qs.q: What is the defining ascitic fluid absolute neutrophil count threshold used to diagnose Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (SBP)?
o: Ascitic absolute neutrophil count greater than 250 cells/ul
Ascitic absolute neutrophil count less than 50 cells/ul
Ascitic absolute neutrophil count exactly 100 cells/ul
Ascitic absolute neutrophil count greater than 500 cells/ul
qs.e: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is defined by an ascitic neutrophil count greater than 250 cells/ul with a pure growth of a single organism and no surgically correctable cause. A lower count would generally rule out this diagnosis.

qs.q: Which of the following organisms is noted as one of the most common causative agents of Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis?
qs.e: E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and pneumococcus are listed as the most common agents responsible for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Anaerobes account for only about 1% of cases.

qs.q: When managing a patient with Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis, what is the recommended action if the ascitic fluid PMN count has not decreased by at least 25% after 2 days of treatment?
o: Double the daily dose of oral spironolactone
Perform an urgent liver transplantation procedure
qs.e: The text states that clinicians should re-evaluate if the ascitic fluid PMN count has not decreased by at least 25% after 2 days of treatment. Stopping antibiotics prematurely without re-evaluation would be clinically inappropriate.

qs.q: What peritoneal fluid polymorphonuclear (PMN) cell count threshold indicates spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP)?
qs.e: A PMN count greater than 250/mm3 in the ascitic fluid analysis indicates spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Elevated WBC counts can also signal general inflammation or infection.
